title: The Log-Likelihood-Ratio Proxy
takeaway: The paper scores every string with a hand-built number: how much more likely that string is under a guessed context (base64, Arabic script, DNA) than under the data as a whole. Because the score is computed from Unicode blocks and character counts, and never from the autoencoder, it gives an outside yardstick for checking whether a feature's proposed interpretation holds.
walkthrough:
This is an unnumbered display, written inline in Section 3 and unpacked in Appendix 12. It defines the [[computational-proxy]] — the score the paper puts next to a feature's activations to test an interpretation.

Read the ratio first. The numerator $P(s|\text{context})$ is the probability of the string $s$ if $s$ really came from the hypothesised context. The denominator $P(s)$ is its probability under the data distribution generally. A ratio above one means the hypothesis explains the string better than the general distribution does; the [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]] takes the log, so "better explained" becomes a positive number.

Now the two pieces, each estimated crudely and on purpose.

The denominator is [[unigram-p-s-estimate]]: $P(s)=\prod_{t\in s}p(t)$, the product of independent per-token unigram probabilities. No context, no ordering — just how common each token is.

The numerator depends on the hypothesis. For the [[base64-proxy]], every base64 character gets probability $1/64$ and everything else $10^{-10}$, multiplied across characters. The [[dna-proxy]] does the same with A, T, C and G at $1/4$ each. The [[arabic-script-proxy]] instead goes through Bayes' rule, using the fact that Arabic script occupies known Unicode blocks: a string of only Arabic characters gets $P(\text{Arabic}|s)=1$, one with any other character gets $10^{-10}$.

Two adjustments matter. A feature may fire more strongly deep into a long string, so the paper maximises the ratio over prefixes ending at the final token. And the paper says it chose log-likelihoods on the intuition that features interact linearly with the logits, so they are pushed to track log-likelihoods — an intuition, not a result.

What this buys: a number computed without touching the [[sparse-autoencoder]]. Feature and proxy can then be correlated — 0.74 for Arabic, 0.8 for DNA once binarised, 0.38 for base64 — and a feature that fires only where a rare, specific proxy fires is hard to call [[polysemanticity|polysemantic]].

The limits are the paper's own. It admits these contexts were cherry-picked because they are easy to model, and where feature and proxy disagree it usually concludes the proxy, not the feature, is wrong.
latex:
\begin{gathered}
\log\!\left(P(s|\text{base64}) \,/\, P(s)\right) \qquad \log\!\left(P(s|\text{Arabic Script}) \,/\, P(s)\right) \\[6pt]
P(s) = \prod_{t\in s} p(t) \\[6pt]
P(s|\text{base64}) = \prod_{c\in s} P(c), \qquad
P(c) = \begin{cases} 1/64 & c \text{ is a base64 character} \\ 10^{-10} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \\[6pt]
P(s|\text{Arabic}) = P(\text{Arabic}|s) \cdot P(s) \,/\, P(\text{Arabic})
\end{gathered}

terms.definition: The string being scored — in practice a token, or a run of tokens ending at the token whose feature activation is under examination. Everything in the proxy is a probability assigned to this string.

The probability of the string under the hypothesised context, i.e. if the text really were base64, Arabic script, DNA or Hebrew. This is the numerator, and it is estimated with a deliberately simple hand-written model of that context.

The context-free probability of the string under the full empirical data distribution. Estimated as a product of independent per-token unigram probabilities, so it carries no information about word order or context.

The proxy itself: the log of how much more likely the string is under the hypothesis than under the general distribution. Positive means the hypothesis explains the string better; the paper picks the log form on the intuition that features, interacting linearly with logits, are pushed to track log-likelihoods.
A token in the string, and its marginal frequency in the training data. The denominator multiplies $p(t)$ over every token of $s$.
A character in the string, and the probability that character gets under the context model. Used for the base64 and DNA numerators, which are products over characters rather than tokens.

The proposed interpretation of a feature, stated as a kind of text the feature is claimed to respond to. The paper builds proxies only for contexts that are easy to model from Unicode blocks or a small character alphabet.
The encoding whose alphabet is [a-zA-Z0-9+/]. The paper models a base64 string as a uniform random draw from those 64 characters.

Sequences of the uppercase letters A, T, C and G, modelled as uniform random strings over that four-letter alphabet. Because single tokens like CAT occur in ordinary text, the DNA proxy is only evaluated on groups of at least two tokens.
Text in the Arabic writing system, detected by whether characters fall in the Arabic Unicode blocks. The numerator is obtained through Bayes' rule rather than a character model.

The probability that a string is Arabic given the string itself, assigned by a rule rather than learned: 1 if every character is in an Arabic Unicode block, and a tiny value otherwise. Shared punctuation and whitespace count as non-Arabic, which makes the proxy miss some genuine Arabic text.
The base rate of Arabic script in the data, estimated by applying the same Unicode-block rule to a random sample of the dataset. It appears as the normaliser in the Bayes-rule form of the numerator.
The distribution of tokens taken independently, ignoring all context. The paper uses it for the denominator of every proxy.

Because a feature may fire more strongly late in a long stretch of the context, the paper computes the ratio for several prefixes ending at the final token and keeps the largest. This also softens the harsh penalty a single stray character imposes on the Unicode-block rule.
Reducing the continuous proxy to a yes/no value based on its sign, done for the DNA feature because the log-probabilities turned out strongly bimodal.
The single number the paper reports when comparing a proxy against a feature's activations, combining specificity and sensitivity while taking activation magnitude into account.
The claim that when the feature is on, the hypothesised context is usually present. The proxy is what makes this checkable at scale.
The claim that when the context is present, the feature is usually on. The paper finds this is often imperfect, with gaps covered by other features.
A unit responding to several unrelated things at once. A feature that fires only where a rare and specific proxy fires cannot be polysemantic in that usual sense.

numbers.meaning: The probability the base64 model gives to each character in the base64 alphabet [a-zA-Z0-9+/], which has 64 members. Uniform, because the paper models base64 as a random string over that alphabet.

The tiny probability assigned to a character outside the base64 alphabet, and likewise to $P(\text{Arabic}|s)$ when a string contains any non-Arabic character. It is a stand-in for zero, chosen so the product stays finite and the log stays defined while still crushing the score.
The probability given to each of A, T, C and G in the DNA model, four letters treated as equally likely.
The value of $P(\text{Arabic}|s)$ when the string consists entirely of Arabic characters — full certainty, by rule rather than by estimate.
Two of the Unicode blocks the paper checks membership in to decide whether a character is Arabic script. They are given as examples, not as the complete list.
The minimum number of tokens the DNA proxy is evaluated over, because single tokens such as CAT occur both in DNA and in ordinary English.

The Pearson correlation between the Arabic script proxy (thresholded at 0) and the activity of feature A/1/3450, over 40 million tokens. The paper calls this substantial while noting the feature misses some Arabic tokens that other features cover.
The Pearson correlation between the binarised DNA proxy and the DNA feature A/1/2937 — the highest of the four, helped by the proxy's clean bimodal split.
The Pearson correlation between the Hebrew script proxy and A/1/416. The paper attributes part of the shortfall to a companion feature, A/1/1016, that covers the \xd7 byte.

The Pearson correlation between the base64 proxy and A/1/2357 — the weakest of the four. The paper reads this as the proxy being too broad, since hexadecimal strings also score highly under it while having a feature of their own.
The number of tokens over which the Arabic feature-proxy correlation was computed.
The share of training tokens that are Arabic script, according to the proxy. Its rarity is what makes a high-specificity result meaningful.
The share of tokens on which A/1/3450 is active that the proxy calls Arabic — against a 0.13% base rate.

How that 81% varies with activation level: 25% where the feature is barely on, rising to 98% above activation 5. The paper uses this spread to argue that specificity holds where it matters, since larger activations have larger effects on predictions.
The activation level for A/1/3450 above which the proxy agrees 98% of the time; the paper treats this as the boundary of the feature's clean upper spectrum.
